rows.answer: The environmental objectives of the EU Taxonomy are climate change mitigation, climate change adaptation, the sustainable use and protection of water and marine resources, the transition to a circular economy, pollution prevention and control, and the protection and restoration of biodiversity and ecosystems [4].

The minimum safeguards require alignment with the OECD Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises and the UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights, including the eight fundamental ILO conventions and the International Bill of Human Rights [1][2].

An economic activity is considered to significantly harm climate change mitigation where it leads to significant greenhouse gas emissions, taking into account the life cycle of its products and services [1].

A company's sustainability reporting must cover the impacts of its activities on people and the environment, and how sustainability matters affect the undertaking. These are the two materiality perspectives under the double materiality principle [3].

Large public-interest entities that are large undertakings and exceed an average of 500 employees must report for financial years starting on or after 1 January 2024 [4]. The same starting date appears in [1] and [3].
The Commission must adopt assurance standards for reasonable assurance of sustainability reporting by means of delegated acts no later than 1 October 2028 [1][3].

Undertakings should prepare the management report in the electronic reporting format specified in Article 3 of Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/815, with sustainability reporting marked up under that format once it is determined [1][2]. The sustainability statement must also be presented in a format that is both human-readable and machine-readable [3].
The medium-term time horizon runs from the end of the short-term reporting period up to 5 years [3].

Regardless of the materiality assessment outcome, the undertaking must always disclose all the Disclosure Requirements and datapoints in ESRS 2 General Disclosures, plus the Disclosure Requirements (and their datapoints) in topical ESRS related to IRO-1 [1][3].

Disclosure Requirement E1-6 – Gross Scopes 1, 2, 3 and Total GHG emissions asks the undertaking to disclose in metric tonnes of CO2eq its gross Scope 1, Scope 2, Scope 3 and total GHG emissions [2][4].

An economic activity counts as an enabling activity when it directly enables other activities to make a substantial contribution to one or more environmental objectives, and it (a) does not lock in assets that undermine long-term environmental goals, considering their economic lifetime, and (b) has a substantial positive environmental impact on the basis of life-cycle considerations [1].

Non-financial undertakings must disclose the proportion of their turnover, the proportion of their capital expenditure, and the proportion of their operating expenditure associated with environmentally sustainable economic activities [1][5].

A third-country undertaking is subject to Union sustainability reporting requirements if it generates a net turnover of more than EUR 150 million in the Union and has a subsidiary undertaking or a branch in the Union [1]. This applies where the EUR 150 million threshold is met at group level (or individual level if group level does not apply) for each of the last two consecutive financial years [2]. For branches, the separate threshold is more than EUR 40 million in net turnover in the preceding financial year [1][3].

The sustainability reporting must first be covered by a **limited assurance engagement**, with the statutory auditor or audit firm expressing an opinion on its compliance with Union requirements. The passage describes this as the starting point of a progressive approach to raising the level of assurance [1].
The Commission had to adopt the first set of sustainability reporting standards by 30 June 2023 [1][5].
The Commission must review the sustainability reporting standards every three years, and the standards are to be reviewed "at least every three years after their date of application" [1][2][3].
EFRAG (the European Financial Reporting Advisory Group) provides technical advice to the Commission on sustainability reporting standards. [2][3][5]
The long-term time horizon is more than 5 years from the end of the reporting period [3]. This is defined in ESRS 1 paragraph 77(c), which is quoted in passage [3].
Disclosure Requirement E1-1 – Transition plan for climate change mitigation covers the undertaking's transition plan for climate change mitigation [1][2].
The GWP values used to calculate CO2-equivalent emissions of non-CO2 gases must be the most recent IPCC values, based on a 100-year time horizon [1].

An economic activity qualifies as environmentally sustainable only if it (a) contributes substantially to one or more environmental objectives, (b) does not significantly harm any environmental objective, (c) is carried out in compliance with the minimum safeguards in Article 18, and (d) complies with Commission-established technical screening criteria [1][3].

An activity with no technologically and economically feasible low-carbon alternative can qualify if it supports the transition to a climate-neutral economy consistent with limiting warming to 1.5°C, and it has greenhouse gas emission levels matching the best performance in its sector, does not hamper low-carbon alternatives, and does not lock in carbon-intensive assets given their economic lifetime [1].

The passages identify the Member State Expert Group on Sustainable Finance as the body "referred to in Regulation (EU) 2020/852," which is the Taxonomy Regulation [5]. They do not explicitly say that the Commission sets it up.

Listed small and medium-sized undertakings may opt out during a two-year transitional period that follows 1 January 2026, which covers financial years starting before 1 January 2028 [3][5]. The passages state this period for listed SMEs, and the 1 January 2028 cutoff also appears in the derogation for SME public-interest entities [1][2].

For the first three years, a company that cannot obtain all the necessary value chain information must explain the efforts it made, the reasons the information could not be obtained, and its plans to obtain it in the future [1][3]. The ESRS transitional provision sets the same three-year period for sustainability reporting under the ESRS [2].
The short-term time horizon is the period the undertaking adopts as its reporting period in its financial statements, measured as of the end of the reporting period [2].

For an actual negative impact, materiality is based on severity; for a potential negative impact, it is based on both severity and likelihood. Severity is assessed by scale, scope, and irremediable character, and for a potential negative human rights impact, severity takes precedence over likelihood [3].

Undertakings or groups that do not exceed an average of 750 employees during the financial year (on a consolidated basis where applicable) may omit the datapoints on Scope 3 emissions and total GHG emissions in the first year of preparing their sustainability statement [1].
Disclosure Requirement E1-7 covers GHG removals and GHG mitigation projects financed through carbon credits. [1][3]
